Guide

What sagu is

Sagu (사구), or four-ball, is the Korean carom game played with two cue balls — white for one player, yellow for the other — and two red object balls, on a pocketless table. A point is a carom: the cue ball has to reach both reds. The two cue balls keep out of each other's way, because touching your opponent's cue ball is a foul.

How this paper is graded

Every diagram has a faint ellipse drawn on the cloth. That is the position zone, and it is what the paper is really about. A shot scores three points for the carom and one point for each ball — the cue ball and both reds — that comes to rest inside the ellipse, so six points are on offer in each position. Play Shot opens the position on the table, you play it, and the simulation scores it straight away. Your best attempt on a shot is the one that counts.

Reading the assessment

The strip at the top shows how many shots you have completed and your percentage of the points available, with an assessment band that climbs from Beginner to Master as the score improves. Reset clears the paper and starts you again.

Prefer to just play? Open a full game of sagu, or compare this paper with the three-cushion and libre exams. All four papers are free and need no account.

Lobby

Shot List

    Basic

    Half ball gathering

    Half ball is the easiest thickness to aim here, so the shot is really a test of pace. Play it as gently as the carom allows and both reds gather back near where the cue ball started, ready for the next point.

    Long corner gathering

    A long trip for the red, so the power has to do two jobs: bring it back across the table and still leave the cue ball short enough to stay in the zone.

    Short angle draw

    Small angles are sensitive here. Draw takes the red around the corner while the cue ball holds on the contact, and the yellow has to be played around rather than into — reaching it is a foul in sagu.

    Long recovery

    A position that comes up constantly: the red has to come back round to the same side of the table as the cue ball. Play it with a tip less than full draw, so you can hit it firmly without the cue ball running away after the contact.

    Full ball

    A fine cut can reach both reds, but full-ball contact with top spin or natural roll is the reliable way to hold the cue ball and gather the reds together.

    Advanced

    Masse

    The dark arts. Raising the butt of the cue is a last resort in most games, and four-ball players reach for it far more often. Bend the cue ball around the yellow — without touching it, which would be a foul — to glance the red at very low pace and leave both balls nursed in the corner.
